Chapter 6: Charity—The Love That Gives Without Asking
You know, there’s a kind of love that doesn’t just happen on its own. It doesn’t grow from shared memories or spark because of some instant connection. This love shows up when all the other kinds feel stretched thin—when affection’s faded, when friendship’s wobbly, or romance has lost its shine. That’s charity—the kind of love that gives without expecting anything back, that forgives without keeping score.
Picture this: a woman sits at her father’s hospital bed, completely worn out after weeks of worry. And, honestly, she’s angry too—old arguments play over in her mind, and resentment feels heavy on her shoulders. But as she watches him sleep, something starts shifting. The anger doesn’t just vanish, but it’s joined by a quiet sense of compassion. She reaches for his hand—not because she wants to, but because he needs her. In that small moment, she’s not acting out of habit or duty, but from something deeper—a willingness to give, even when it hurts.
Charity isn’t about liking someone, or even feeling close to them. It’s about noticing their need and choosing to respond, even if there’s nothing in it for you. Most of the time, charity slides by unnoticed, because it doesn’t call attention to itself. Think of that neighbor who shovels your driveway without a word, the friend who lets a careless comment go, or the stranger who offers a bit of kindness on a rough day.
This kind of love isn’t easy. It goes against our instincts—asks us to let go of pride, to stop clinging to the need to be right. It encourages us to see others not as competition or burdens, but as fellow travelers, each carrying their own struggles, each deserving of kindness. Charity doesn’t magically erase pain or make life simple, but it does open a door to healing like nothing else can.
Of course, there’s always a risk. Charity can be misunderstood, or even rejected. Sometimes, the people you’re trying to help don’t want your help, or maybe they take advantage of your kindness. It’s easy to feel discouraged—to wonder if any of it is worth it. But charity isn’t about getting results—it’s about the willingness to give, to keep showing up, even when it’s tough.
Over time, charity changes the giver just as much as the receiver. It starts to soften resentment, loosens the grip of fear, and makes space for hope. It’s not just a passing feeling—it’s a choice you make, again and again. And while it might never be perfect, it’s the only kind of love that truly stands the test of time.
